records.Etymology: 115. ‘Butterfly’ and ‘flying-fluttering’ (a) Deog. phiphṛi and phimphṛi ‘butterfly’, Kṭg. phímpəṛi ‘butterfly’ (wrongly put in the Addenda and Corrigenda sub pipīlá- ‘ant’ [8201]), Khaśdh. putuṛi ‘butterfly’, Ku. purputaī ‘butterfly’, Jaun. pōtōṭhō, Him. phĩphṛī, Khāśi. phāphṛi, Pāḍ. pāpṛi, Bhal. papṛi, pepri, Khaś. phāphṛi, Bhad. pāpṛi or pepṛõ all ‘butterfly’ — Kurkh. pəpəla ‘butterfly’ — Paṭṭ. phərphitig ‘butterfly’, Chin. pharphiṭig (or phārpitig, Kaul [2006 ii: 42]) ‘butterfly’, Gar. phremolig ‘butterfly’, K. pam pũ̄par ‘butterfly’ (Sachdeva et al. [2010: 60]) — Ind. phirphirì̄ ‘butterfly’, Bur. asqúriṅe phirán ‘butterfly’, Tor.cail. pʌrparʌk ‘moth’, Paš. pheṭiyák ‘butterfly’ — Psht. parkai ‘butterfly’ — Khet. phōpuṭ ‘butterfly’, S. popṭu ‘butterfly’, Jaṭ. popaṭ ‘butterfly, moth’ and bhabbaṭ ‘moth’, Ko.S. phulpã̄khrũ ‘butterfly’ (with second component < OIA pakṣín- ‘bird’), Ko.kaṇ. birbirẽ ‘butterfly’ — Sad. paplā ‘butterfly’ and Kh. pampla, phamphlaʔ which seems (like first word in K. pam pũ̄par) to have Austro-Asiatic parallels: Bahnaric Cua pʌm pil ‘moth, butterfly’, Proto-Vietic *paːmə ‘butterfly’, Sant. pipṛiaṅ ‘butterfly’ and Bon. laʔlaʔp ‘butterfly’, and Mon-Khmer LwAd. poopil ‘butterfly’. Perhaps also related are Kho. pulmuṇḍuk ‘butterfly’, Sh.gur. phōpal ‘butterfly’, Wkh. pilek-miˈlek or pilpilak ‘butterfly’ and Ishk. parparanuk ‘butterfly’, Kamd. prüšpˈulik ‘butterfly; moth’, Bal. pirrik ‘butterfly’. Cf. PIE *pelpel- ‘butterfly’, Latin pāpiliō, Arm. xipilik (loanword?), all ‘butterfly’; cf. also Common Kartvelian *perpel-‘butterfly; wing’, Zan (Laz dialect) parpal-i, Megrelian parpal-ia//parpal-i ‘butterfly; twisting/swirling’; cf. also PTB *pur ‘butterfly’ which, however, is not found in Tib., the only geographically plausible near form is Kann. pʰərpʰitig ‘butterfly’. Generally one can say that many of the above forms got not only ‘indianized’ i.e. they are examples for linguistic naturalization (on this term see p. 223), but also intersected with similar-sounding words e.g. from Austro-Asiatic and Dravidian, and last but not least some of the words may have also been influenced by reflexes of OIA pattrá- ‘wing’ with -ṭṭ- extension (7733) and by the following lemma (b). Cf. also Proto-Dravidian *papla ‘butterfly’ (Pfeiffer [1972: 20f.]) and e.g. Ora. paplā ‘butterfly’, and simimlar “sound-symbolism” forms in Munda (Kuiper [1962: 82]). (b) Bng., Deog. and West Pahāṛī far ‘the sound of a bird’s flight’, Khaśdh. phʌr-phʌr ‘ditto’, Garh. phurr ‘sound of a flying bird’ and pharṛī ‘a banner’, N. pharpharāhaṭ, phyār-phyār, pher-pher all ‘fluttering’ and Khm. phur phur ‘high in the air’, Rab. furut ‘sound of flying away a bird’ (Roy [2011: 100]) — Jaḍ. phur-phurja ‘to fly’ (Z.), Pur. phurcas ‘to fly’ (with infinitive/verbal noun ending), Balt., Nyam-kad and Tib. phur ‘(to) fly’ (other Tibetan forms are phir-, bur-, ur-), New. pharphar, phyār phyār ‘fluttering’ — Brah. firfir and paṛpaṛ ‘flutter; fluttering’ — Ind. phʌ́r ho- ‘to fly’, also in some Sh. dialects puř- and phuri- ‘fly’, Kho. pár ‘sound of bird’s wings flapping’, Bur.ys. pər ɛt- ‘to fly’ — Rj.jaip. bharbhar ‘the noise made by the flying of a bird’ — H. phurr ‘whirring sound (of wings)’ — Sant. phur phur ‘making buzzing, whirring sounds’ (one of Bodding’s examples is with a quail). There is certainly an onomatopoeic component in this lemma and it is unclear to which extend the Tibetan verb was borrowed into surrounding languages. Note also Pers. parper ‘fluttering’, and there are more similar Munda forms: reflexes of Proto-Kherwarian apir ‘to fly’ are found in several modern Munda languages and in Nih. aphir ‘to fly’ (Pinnow [K 501]). Whether or not there is IE influence in this lemma is difficult to say. Influence of OIA *spharati¹ ‘throbs, quivers’ (13820) and of sphuráti¹ ‘spurns, darts’ (13849)  can be excluded because of the different semantic reflexes in Bng. phɔrphɔrāṇɔ ‘to whirl or swirl up (as wind)’ and phurṇɔ ‘to twitch, bat (eye[lash], muscle)’. But it is clear that it is another example of what Mallory and Adams (already quoted above p. 778) describe as an instance “where onomatopoeia has supported their survival.” Cf. also PN *pʰar- ‘to flutter, fly’ (CINCL 101), PAA *par ‘to fly’ (also reflected in PMU **pER) and even Swab. pfurren ‘to flare up with whooshing, buzzing speed’ (von Schmid).

records.Etymology: 149. Bng. migṇɔ n.m. ‘(quick) blinking (with eyes)’ (with -ṇɔ2 suffix), e.g. seu migṇɔ kɔrɛ ‘he blinks’ (lit.‘he does blinking’), and miṅg-miṅg gaṛṇɔ ‘to blink (with the eyes)’ (with gaṛṇɔ ‘to pull out’) — Klm. ečämik HL n.f. ‘wink or blink of the eye’ (← ec̣ H(L) ‘eyes’) cf. PIE *meigʰ- (perhaps also *meik-) ‘close the eyes’. Sub OIA *micc- ‘close the eyes, blink’ (10118) there are also modern reflexes with -kk- extensions like H. mickānā ‘to wink’; according to Turner, “[a] non-Aryan or widespread onom. word, scarcely. . . to be assigned to a common IE. root. . . ” See also EWA sub MEṢ ‘to open the eyes’ (CDIAL MIṢ *‘blink, open the eyes’) regarding the complexity of this lemma and note also Dravidian Kurkh. miṅkh- ‘to close the eyes’ (Pfeiffer [1972: 28]). Directly related to 10118 are Bng. miċṇɔ ‘to blink; to close one’s eyes’ and mɔċrɔ2 ‘blinking (with eyes)’ (not to be confused with almost identically pronounced mɔċrɔ1 ‘drunk’ which is < OIA matsará- ‘exhilarating’ [9756] [Pa., Pk.] without known modern parallels). Since it is quite impossible that Bng. migṇɔ or miṅg-miṅg gaṛṇɔ is a -kk- extension of miċṇɔ, we have here yet another case of semantic-morphological amalgamations with the Bng. and Klm. forms closest to PIE. Regarding Bng. miṅg- miṅg gaṛṇɔ cf. e.g. Lith. mingù ‘to fall asleep’ (or rather miñga ‘falls asleep’) and see Derksen’s discussion of Proto-Baltic *migla ‘mist, haze’ and *migti ‘fall asleep’ (2015: 317).
